werk/2pac-still-i-rise.text:
Still I Rise was released on 21 December 1999 by Interscope Records as a collaboration between 2Pac and the Outlawz. The album consists of unreleased but reworked material, mostly from the time he was signed to Death Row Records. Part of the original Outlawz line-up is missing: Hussein Fatal had left because he refused to sign with Death Row.

Production came from his regular producers Tony Pizarro, Johnny J and QDIII. Big Syke and Nate Dogg appear as guests. The only single was Baby Don't Cry (Keep Ya' Head Up II), with the female group H.E.A.T. Letter to the President can be heard in the 2001 film Training Day. The album entered the US Billboard 200 at number 7 and later went platinum.
werk/2pac-still-i-rise.listen: Listen to Baby Don't Cry (Keep Ya' Head Up II) and notice the role of the female singers alongside the rapping.

werk/2pac-strictly-4-my-n-i-g-g-a-z.text:
His second solo album was released in February 1993, after the success of the film Juice. It was recorded in Richmond, Los Angeles and New York. A follow-up to his debut had already been planned in early 1992, but Time Warner rejected it after an uproar over the lyrics. Several tracks from it, such as Keep Ya Head Up, I Get Around and The Streetz R Deathrow, ended up on this album.

It sounds less underground than the first album and became his breakthrough. It contains commentary on social issues and on Dan Quayle, who had criticised the rapper for his violent lyrics. The singles Holler If Ya Hear Me, I Get Around, Keep Ya Head Up and Papa'z Song each received a video. Critics were largely positive. Greg Tate called it his best-constructed and most political album. According to AllMusic, the production occasionally falters, but the record presents a rapper who is growing.
werk/2pac-strictly-4-my-n-i-g-g-a-z.listen: Listen to Keep Ya Head Up and notice how guest singer Dave Hollister complements the rapping.

werk/a-ha-east-of-the-sun-west-of-the-mo.text:
East of the Sun, West of the Moon was released on 22 October 1990 as the fourth album by the Norwegian synth-pop band a-ha. The title comes from a Norwegian fairy tale. The album was released on Warner Bros. Records and was shared between two producers: Christopher Neil and Ian Stanley, who had previously played with Tears for Fears.

The mood is darker and more atmospheric than on the earlier records, on which the group had still sounded more radio-friendly. In Norway the album reached number one, and in several European countries and in Japan it reached the top 20. Critics were divided. Entertainment Weekly found the synthesizers bloated, whereas AllMusic called it a carefully crafted collection of songs, beautifully sung and full of echoes and suggestion. According to that reviewer, the album deserved a better reception than it received. On The Way We Talk, keyboard player Magne Furuholmen sings lead vocals himself.
werk/a-ha-east-of-the-sun-west-of-the-mo.listen: Listen to The Way We Talk and notice the voice: here the lead vocals are sung not by Morten Harket but by Magne Furuholmen. Can you hear how that different voice gives the song a colour of its own?

werk/a-ha-hunting-high-and-low.text:
Hunting High and Low is the debut album by the Norwegian synth-pop band a-ha. It was released on 1 June 1985 in Norway and the United States, and at the end of October in Europe. The group recorded it at Eel Pie Studios in Twickenham, London, with the producers Tony Mansfield, John Ratcliff and Alan Tarney.

Take On Me had been released earlier without success. It was re-recorded for the album, and with a new video by Steve Barron it became a number 1 in the US Hot 100. The Sun Always Shines on T.V., Train of Thought and the title song followed. The band became the first Norwegian group to be nominated for a Grammy for Best New Artist. AllMusic called the album cohesive, with clever changes of tempo.
werk/a-ha-hunting-high-and-low.listen: Listen to Take On Me and notice the synthesizer riff that carries the song, and how high the singer goes in the chorus.

werk/a-ha-scoundrel-days.text:
Scoundrel Days is a-ha's second album, released in 1986. The songs were written by Pål Waaktaar and Magne Furuholmen; singer Morten Harket contributed nothing to the writing this time. The two writers produced three tracks themselves: I've Been Losing You, Maybe, Maybe and Soft Rains of April.

The sound is built on synthesizers such as the Yamaha DX7 and the Roland Juno, supplemented by a Fairlight and a PPG Wave. Manhattan Skyline begins quietly and switches in the chorus to a hard-rock-style guitar riff. I've Been Losing You became the most successful single in Europe and Cry Wolf entered the US Hot 100. The album sold more than six million copies. AllMusic particularly praised the first two tracks, Scoundrel Days and The Swing of Things.
werk/a-ha-scoundrel-days.listen: Listen to Manhattan Skyline and notice the contrast between the quiet verse and the hard chorus.

werk/a-ha-stay-on-these-roads.text:
Stay on These Roads came out on 3 May 1988 and is a-ha's third studio album. The producer was Alan Tarney. The record was made with a battery of synthesizers, including a Synclavier, a Prophet 5, a DX-7 and a Roland D-50, and with a drum machine. Morten Harket sings, Magne Furuholmen plays keyboards and Paul Waaktaar plays guitar.

The album was once again a major international hit and, like its two predecessors, reached number two in Britain. Six singles were released from it, including the title track, The Blood That Moves the Body, Touchy! and You Are the One. It also contains a new version of The Living Daylights, the theme song the band had made for a James Bond film. NME heard mainly wistfulness in Waaktaar's lyrics: they are about crying, leaving and longing.
werk/a-ha-stay-on-these-roads.listen: Listen to Stay On These Roads and notice how synthesizers and voice together create a wistful atmosphere.

werk/a-r-rahman-raunaq.text:
Raunaq, from 2014, grew out of a meeting between the composer A. R. Rahman and Kapil Sibal, who wrote poems. In 2013 the composer was given a book of paintings by Raja Ravi Varma as a gift, and he wanted the videos to use images from those paintings. When Sibal showed him his collection, he became fascinated by seven or eight poems. About six months before March 2014 he began setting them to music, with the support of Sony Music.

The album has seven tracks and portrays Indian society, blended with the lyricist's personal experiences. Aabhi Jaa is about love and parting, and Laadli is a tribute to all the women of the country. For Laadli the composer felt that Lata Mangeshkar was the right voice. The album was released on 1 September 2014 and dedicated to Vogue Empower, an initiative for women's empowerment.
werk/a-r-rahman-raunaq.listen: Listen to Laadli and notice the voice of Lata Mangeshkar: does her voice suit a tribute to women?

werk/a-tribe-called-quest-midnight-marau.text:
Midnight Marauders is the third album by A Tribe Called Quest, released in November 1993. The recording took nine months and took place in New York studios such as Battery Studios. Q-Tip made a large part of the beats in the basement of Phife Dawg's grandmother's house. After The Low End Theory, the group felt the pressure to repeat that success. Q-Tip produced most of it himself, with help from, among others, Large Professor and DJ Ali Shaheed Muhammad.

The sound is rougher and funkier than on the previous record, with samples from jazz, funk, soul and R&B and many horn melodies. Q-Tip deliberately left the noise in the samples. The lyrics are socially aware, positive and full of humour. Critics were largely positive. Writers have since come to regard the album as a high point of the Native Tongues movement and of 1990s hip hop.
werk/a-tribe-called-quest-midnight-marau.listen: In Award Tour, listen to the bass line and the way the two rappers alternate. Notice how smoothly the beat keeps rolling.

werk/a-tribe-called-quest-people-s-insti.text:
The debut was released in April 1990 on Jive Records. A Tribe Called Quest came from Queens and, together with the Jungle Brothers and De La Soul, formed the Native Tongues collective. Record labels initially did not want the group, because their image and sound were too idiosyncratic. Only after the success of 3 Feet High and Rising, on which Q-Tip could be heard, did a contract follow. Recording began at Calliope Studios at the end of 1989 and took three months. There Q-Tip learned to work with samplers and arranged almost everything himself, while Ali Shaheed Muhammad played the instruments and cut the scratches.

The sound is relaxed and playful. Q-Tip used jazz, R&B and rock that other producers ignored, and added crying children, frogs and Hawaiian strings. The lyrics sound like ordinary conversation. Critics were full of praise and the record is regarded as a cornerstone of alternative hip hop. It influenced many artists in hip hop and R&B.
werk/a-tribe-called-quest-people-s-insti.listen: Listen to Bonita Applebum, one of the first tracks recorded for the album: notice how loose and conversational the rapping sounds against the calm backing.

werk/a-tribe-called-quest-the-low-end-th.text:
The Low End Theory is the second album by A Tribe Called Quest and was released in September 1991 on Jive Records. It was recorded mainly at Battery Studios in New York, directly after the debut. Rapper Phife Dawg had just learned that he had diabetes, and the group decided to give him a larger role. Q-Tip produced most of it himself, with Ali Shaheed Muhammad behind the turntables.

The sound is minimalist and consists of bass, drum breaks and jazz samples, with influences from bebop and hard bop. In the lyrics, social criticism, wordplay and humour alternate, with a lively interplay between Q-Tip and Phife Dawg. At first critics and the people at Jive doubted its commercial success, but Jazz (We've Got) and Scenario attracted a great deal of attention. The album is regarded as a milestone of alternative hip hop and launched the careers of artists such as Busta Rhymes.
werk/a-tribe-called-quest-the-low-end-th.listen: In Check the Rhime, listen to the conversation between Q-Tip and Phife Dawg: they pick up each other's lines over a calm, loose beat.

werk/abba-arrival.text:
When ABBA began work on their fourth album in August 1975, the group was only moderately well known worldwide. Arrival brought their international breakthrough. Recording ran until September 1976 at Metronome and Glen studios in Stockholm. The first track to go into the studio was Boogaloo, inspired by the disco sound of the moment. With new lyrics it became Dancing Queen, later the group's biggest hit. Knowing Me, Knowing You and Money, Money, Money also came from this record.

The songs were tinkered with a great deal. My Love My Life became a lush ballad with backing vocals inspired by I'm Not in Love by 10cc. The last track to be recorded was an instrumental piece that was first called Ode to Dalecarlia and was given the title of the album. In 1977 Arrival was the best-selling album in the United Kingdom. In 2024 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.
werk/abba-arrival.listen: Listen to Dancing Queen and notice how the song reveals its origins in the disco sound of the time.

werk/abba-dancing-queen.text: On 16 August 1976 ABBA released Dancing Queen. After a piano glissando, the song begins not with a verse but with a piece of the chorus: You can dance, you can jive. The listener hears the strongest moment straight away. Only then does the verse follow, about a Friday night on the dance floor. It was ABBA's only number one in America. Benny and Björn worked like a hit factory of their own.
werk/abba-dancing-queen.listen: The chorus begins even before the verse. A hit that starts right at its strongest point.

werk/abba-ring-ring.text:
Ring Ring is ABBA's debut and was released on 26 March 1973 in Scandinavia, still under the name Björn & Benny, Agnetha & Frida. The first recording, People Need Love, dates from the spring of 1972, when the four were still working on all kinds of other projects. Only after the title song became a hit did they decide to continue together permanently. Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus wrote almost all the songs and produced the record.

The original Swedish release opens with the Swedish version of Ring Ring. On the international releases the English version comes first. She's My Kind of Girl dates from 1969 and became a hit in Japan. Disillusion is the only song on one of the group's studio albums that Agnetha Fältskog co-wrote. The album reached the top ten in Sweden, Norway and Australia and was not released in England until 1992.
werk/abba-ring-ring.listen: Listen to Disillusion, the only song on one of the group's studio albums that Agnetha Fältskog co-wrote, and notice her singing.

werk/abba-super-trouper.text:
In January 1980, Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson travelled to Barbados to write new songs. Recording at Polar Studios in Stockholm then continued throughout the year, with a break for a short tour of Japan. The title was settled early on; the title track itself was not written until October in the studio. It was the last album ABBA recorded while Anni-Frid Lyngstad and Benny Andersson were still married.

After the disco era of Voulez-Vous, the group sounded more straightforwardly pop again. The big single was The Winner Takes It All, partly about Björn and Agnetha's broken marriage. Lay All Your Love On Me is electronic dance music, and The Piper has lyrics inspired by a novel by Stephen King. The album received a positive reception and is regarded by some as their best studio record.
werk/abba-super-trouper.listen: Listen to Lay All Your Love On Me and notice how the electronic, danceable backing relates to the vocals.

werk/abba-voulez-vous.text:
Voulez-Vous was released on 23 April 1979 and is ABBA's sixth studio album. The recording went with difficulty. After six months only two tracks were finished, and tension within the group was rising. During that time the group opened its own Polar Studios in Stockholm. Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus then withdrew to the Bahamas, where the title song and Kisses of Fire were written. They recorded the basic tracks of Voulez-Vous in Miami with the disco band Foxy, the only time the group recorded outside Sweden.

The record heads for the dance floor, and the cover was shot in a Stockholm nightclub. Chiquitita, Does Your Mother Know, I Have a Dream and Voulez-Vous/Angeleyes became hits. Critics were largely positive, although one reviewer found the album neat but clinical. In England it stayed at number one for a month.
werk/abba-voulez-vous.listen: Listen to I Have a Dream and notice the children's choir from the International School of Stockholm singing along.

werk/abba-waterloo.text: On 6 April 1974, ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest in Brighton with Waterloo. The writers were Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus, together with their manager Stig Anderson. They had listened closely to Phil Spector and British glam rock. In the years that followed they made hit after hit in Stockholm, with a sound that worked in any language, sung by Agnetha Fältskog and Anni-Frid Lyngstad. Sweden became a hit-making nation.
werk/abba-waterloo.listen: Hear the piano, the saxophone and the chorus that sticks in your head at once: a battle as a love story.

werk/abbey-lincoln-it-s-magic.text:
It's Magic is the third album by the singer Abbey Lincoln. She recorded it in New York in 1958 for the Riverside label, in two sessions on 24 July and 15 August. She sings with a large ensemble of jazz musicians, including the trumpeters Kenny Dorham and Art Farmer, the saxophonist Benny Golson, the pianist Wynton Kelly and the drummer Philly Joe Jones.

The album contains classics of the American repertoire, such as the title song by Sammy Cahn and Jule Styne and Exactly Like You. Out of the Past is by Golson, with lyrics by Jon Hendricks, and Little Niles is by Randy Weston. Scott Yanow of AllMusic gave it four and a half stars. According to John Fordham in The Guardian, she here picks up the urgency of the civil rights movement, and the sharpness of a freer jazz that was still to come.
werk/abbey-lincoln-it-s-magic.listen: Listen to Ain't Nobody's Business and notice how every phrase is sung with emphasis, so that the lyrics really come across.

werk/abc-alphabet-city.text:
After a two-year break, during which singer Martin Fry was treated for Hodgkin's disease, ABC recorded this fourth album. The recording took nine months and was done at Marcus Recording Studios in London, with the help of Bernard Edwards, best known from Chic. The title and several songs refer to Alphabet City, the neighbourhood in Manhattan where Fry and Mark White lived for a time.

Fry said at the time that, after records that had left people confused, the band wanted to make an overview of everything it had done before. When Smokey Sings is a tribute to Smokey Robinson and reached number eleven in the British singles chart. The Night You Murdered Love and King Without a Crown were also released as singles. The album reached number seven in the United Kingdom, the first top ten since the debut The Lexicon of Love.
werk/abc-alphabet-city.listen: Listen to When Smokey Sings and notice the strings, which Richard Niles arranged for this song. Does the sound suit a tribute to Smokey Robinson?

werk/abc-beauty-stab.text:
After the success of The Lexicon of Love, ABC did not want to make a sequel. In August and September 1983 the band recorded the second album, over three months and in studios in London, including Sarm and Abbey Road. The group produced it themselves, together with Gary Langan, who had also engineered the debut. The rhythm section was drummer Andy Newmark and bassist Alan Spenner, who had recently played with Roxy Music.

The sound now revolves around guitars rather than the smooth, orchestrated production of the debut. According to The Guardian, the strings had been replaced by solid guitars. Most critics reacted negatively, and a journalist later called it one of the great career-sabotaging records in pop history. The album reached number 12 in England, and singer Martin Fry later said that a sequel might actually have been the wise choice. Founder Stephen Singleton left the band shortly after the promotion.
werk/abc-beauty-stab.listen: Listen to That Was Then But This Is Now and notice the guitars. Compare that with the smooth pop you would expect from the debut.

werk/abc-how-to-be-a-zillionaire.text:
How to Be a ... Zillionaire! was released in October 1985 and is the third album by the English pop band ABC. It was the only record on which the founders Martin Fry and Mark White worked with the new members Eden and David Yarritu. The two appeared on the cover as performers and had little or no musical input. The foursome were depicted as cartoon characters, on the cover and in the videos, and wore striking costumes and played fake instruments at mimed performances.

Four singles were released: How to Be a Millionaire, Be Near Me, Vanity Kills and Ocean Blue. Be Near Me did best in the United States, where it reached number nine. The album itself reached number 28 in the United Kingdom. In 2005 a digitally remastered CD with eight bonus tracks was released.
werk/abc-how-to-be-a-zillionaire.listen: Listen to Be Near Me, the album's biggest American hit, and notice the vocals and the structure of the song.

werk/abdullah-ibrahim-african-sketchbook.text:
African Sketchbook was recorded on 16 May 1969 at Radio Bern, under the direction of producer Horst Weber. The album was released on LP on Enja Records. Pianist Abdullah Ibrahim wrote all the pieces himself and plays flute on the first track, Air. On the other pieces he sits at the piano. It is therefore a solo record, with short, varied pieces.

According to the AllMusic reviewer, the recording quality leaves something to be desired, but the music more than makes up for it. He recommends the album above all to listeners who know Ibrahim's later work and not yet his early period. The Penguin Guide to Jazz called the record as fragmentary as the title suggests.
werk/abdullah-ibrahim-african-sketchbook.listen: Listen to Air and notice the flute: Ibrahim does not play piano here. Then compare it with one of the piano pieces, such as Mamma.

werk/abdullah-ibrahim-good-news-from-afr.text:
Good News from Africa is an album of duets by pianist Abdullah Ibrahim, then still known as Dollar Brand, and bassist Johnny Dyani. They recorded it on 10 December 1973 at Tonstudio Bauer in Ludwigsburg. It was released in 1974 on the Swiss label Cameo and the German Enja.

The record mixes traditional African pieces with Ibrahim's own compositions. According to AllMusic, Islamic chants also appear, and both musicians sing along movingly. The Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings heard duos moving from dark, almost tragic pessimism to a jubilant, exultant climax. One reviewer called the album a personal celebration of a newly found faith. AllMusic spoke of one of the most beautiful recordings of the 1970s.
werk/abdullah-ibrahim-good-news-from-afr.listen: Listen to Adhan & Allah-O-Akbar and notice the voices of the two musicians. Hear how singing is just as important here as piano and bass.

werk/ac-dc-back-in-black.text:
Back in Black was released on 25 July 1980 and was AC/DC's seventh studio album. After the breakthrough with Highway to Hell, a follow-up was planned, but in February 1980 singer Bon Scott died after a night out in London. The remaining members considered stopping, but carried on and chose Brian Johnson, formerly the singer of Geordie, as their new frontman. Johnson wrote the album together with the brothers Angus and Malcolm Young. Producer Robert John Lange, who had also produced Highway to Hell, recorded it in seven weeks in the Bahamas.

The cover is completely black, as a sign of mourning for Scott. The album was an enormous success with the public and critics, and was followed by a year-long world tour that made the band one of the most popular of the early 1980s. Since then it has appeared on countless lists of the best albums.
werk/ac-dc-back-in-black.listen: Listen to Back in Black and notice how the guitar riff carries the song and how the vocals sit sharply on top of it.

werk/ac-dc-high-voltage.text:
High Voltage is AC/DC's first album to be released internationally, on 14 May 1976 on Atlantic. It was compiled from the two Australian albums High Voltage and T.N.T. from 1975, the second of which supplied most of the tracks. Producers George Young and Harry Vanda gave the band its sound. Young cut It's a Long Way to the Top down from a long jam and came up with the bagpipes. Singer Bon Scott, in reality a drummer, had to learn the instrument. The oi chant in T.N.T. was also Young's idea.

In the lyrics Scott writes about the good and bad sides of the rock life. Live Wire opened the band's shows for years. In England in 1976 the band was wrongly mistaken for punk. Rolling Stone called the album a low point of hard rock, but in the United States three million copies were sold.
werk/ac-dc-high-voltage.listen: Listen to It's a Long Way to the Top and notice the bagpipes among the guitars. How does that instrument fit a rock song?

werk/ac-dc-highway-to-hell.text:
By 1978 AC/DC had released five albums and toured extensively, but Atlantic Records in America wanted a more radio-friendly sound. The first producer, Eddie Kramer, clashed with the band. Then came Mutt Lange, and with him the sixth album. From 24 March to 14 April 1979 the band worked at Roundhouse Studios in London, often fifteen hours a day, honing the songs. Lange, himself a trained singer, taught Bon Scott to breathe better and also sang along on the melodic backing vocals. That polish did not take away the band's rough sound.

The title track is the best-known song. Atlantic did not like the title, but Angus Young explained that it describes the experience of touring. Lange had Angus play his solo beside him and pointed out the notes on the guitar neck. It was the last album with Bon Scott, who died on 19 February 1980.
werk/ac-dc-highway-to-hell.listen: Listen to the guitar solo in Highway to Hell. Can you hear that the solo stays short and catchy?

werk/ac-dc-let-there-be-rock.text:
At the end of 1976 AC/DC were in a slump. Things were going well in London and Europe, but Atlantic Records in America did not think the album Dirty Deeds was good enough and threatened to drop the band. The group responded combatively. Angus Young recounted that his brother George, who produced together with Harry Vanda, asked what kind of album they wanted to make, and that the answer was: lots of guitar riffs, after all that touring. The result came out in March 1977 in Australasia. In July an adapted international version followed, with the later famous logo by Gerard Huerta.

It was the last album with bassist Mark Evans. Critics were very positive. AllMusic called it sweaty, dirty rock and one of the best records of the Bon Scott era. In 2001 Q included it among the heaviest albums ever. According to one biographer, it made the band an album band.
werk/ac-dc-let-there-be-rock.listen: Listen to Bad Boy Boogie and notice Bon Scott's vocals and Angus Young's guitar solo.

werk/acda-en-de-munnik-het-regent-zonnes.text: In 1998 Het regent zonnestralen by Acda en de Munnik was released, the duo of Thomas Acda and Paul de Munnik. They came from the theatre and played in theatres, with guitars and piano, personal songs with lyrics you had to be able to follow. Here the line continues that began with the kleinkunst tradition (Dutch cabaret song) and Boudewijn de Groot: singable songs, with a guitar, in their own language.
werk/acda-en-de-munnik-het-regent-zonnes.listen: Hear the acoustic guitars and the two voices alternating in a personal song.

werk/adele-21.text:
Adele began her second album in April 2009, named after her age while making it. She wanted a more cheerful and contemporary sound than on 19, but the first sessions yielded little. Only Take It All, produced by Jim Abbiss, remained. When her relationship ended, she wrote new songs in a rush of emotion, including with Paul Epworth and Ryan Tedder. Rick Rubin was involved with one demo.

The album builds on the soul and Motown of her debut, with influences from American country and blues. With Rolling in the Deep, an a cappella verse came first, after which Epworth improvised a melody on acoustic guitar and a pounding drum imitated the beating of her heart. Label expectations were modest, but the album topped the charts in more than thirty countries. It was praised for its restrained production and the singing, and in 2012 it won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
werk/adele-21.listen: Listen to Rolling In the Deep and notice the pounding drum that imitates the beating of a heart.

werk/adele-25.text:
After the success of 21, Adele thought for a while about giving up music. In 2012 she announced a break, and after the birth of her son in October 2012 she felt like recording again. The first sessions stalled because of writer's block. Only when her son was a year and a half old did she return to the studio. She did not want to make a second 21, nor a new heartbreak album.

The album was released on 20 November 2015 and is described as a make-up record. The lyrics are about nostalgia for the past, the passing of time, motherhood, new love and regret. Unlike before, the production uses electronic elements, inventive rhythms, organs and influences from 1980s R&B. Hello became an international number 1. Critics praised the production and the singing. The album won the Grammy for Album of the Year and became the best-selling album of 2015.
werk/adele-25.listen: Listen to Hello and notice how the voice grows from piano and restrained backing into a big, powerful chorus.

werk/adele-someone-like-you.text: In January 2011 Adele released Someone Like You, from the album 21. She wrote it with the American songwriter Dan Wilson, in two days. The song uses the same chord changes as Let It Be, I-V-vi-IV, but in A, and the piano plays the chords as a rolling motion. After a performance at the Brit Awards it became a number one in England and then in America.
werk/adele-someone-like-you.listen: Hear the piano playing each chord as separate notes one after another, an arpeggio, beneath Adele's voice.

werk/aerosmith-draw-the-line.text:
In 1977 Aerosmith were at the height of their popularity. Toys in the Attic and Rocks had made the band famous, but the heavy touring and drug use were taking their toll. For the fifth album the band moved in March, with producer Jack Douglas, to The Cenacle, a former convent near New York. There the Record Plant installed a studio. In Kings and Queens the drums stood on the altar of the chapel, while Douglas hit the snare from the confessional.

Tyler and Perry were less involved than before, so other band members also contributed to the writing. The sound is straightforward hard rock, with Draw the Line as one of the wildest songs. The cover is a caricature of the band by Al Hirschfeld. Critics were divided in 1977; later opinion was milder. Perry himself called the album the beginning of the end.
werk/aerosmith-draw-the-line.listen: Listen to Draw the Line and notice the bass guitar lick on which the song turns: according to Tyler, it made the song almost write itself. Hear how the vocals come in over it.

werk/aerosmith-get-your-wings.text:
Aerosmith's debut from January 1973 went almost unnoticed: no press, no radio, no reviews. The band responded by touring heavily and building an audience that way. In December 1973 they went to the Record Plant in New York to record a second album, for the first time with producer Jack Douglas, who would go on to make three more albums with the group.

Many songs had already been tried out in the rehearsal room and on stage. Train Kept a Rollin' was an old favourite from the live set, with a stop-start groove that came out of jamming during soundchecks. Lord of the Thighs was written last, because a song was still missing, and is about the seedy neighbourhood around the studio. The album produced three singles, but none of them reached the charts.
werk/aerosmith-get-your-wings.listen: Listen to Train Kept a Rollin' and notice the groove that keeps pausing and then rolling on again.

werk/aerosmith-rocks.text:
Rocks is Aerosmith's fourth studio album and was released on 13 May 1976 on Columbia. After the breakthrough with Toys in the Attic, the band, together with producer Jack Douglas, wanted to make a genuine hard rock record, as raw and live-sounding as possible. They drove the Record Plant's mobile recording truck into their rehearsal space and recorded almost all the basic tracks there. Guitarist Brad Whitford and Tom Hamilton contributed more to the writing than before.

Joe Perry wrote the opener Back in the Saddle on a six-string bass guitar. The riff falls outside the usual rock formula. The record produced three singles, of which Back in the Saddle and Last Child reached the top 40. AllMusic says the group sounds at its rawest and most rocking here. In 2020 Rolling Stone placed the record at number 366 among the greatest albums of all time, and Guns N' Roses, Metallica and Nirvana were influenced by it.
werk/aerosmith-rocks.listen: Listen to Back in the Saddle and notice the low, strange riff that Joe Perry came up with on a six-string bass.

werk/aerosmith-toys-in-the-attic.text:
Toys in the Attic was released on 8 April 1975 on Columbia Records and was Aerosmith's third album. Producer Jack Douglas, who had already worked on the previous record Get Your Wings, almost became the sixth member of the group during the recording. The band had toured for a year and sounded tighter. After two albums with songs from the clubs, they now started from scratch: for the first time most of the material was written during recording, after months of preparation.

The album contains well-known songs such as Walk This Way, Sweet Emotion and the title song. Sweet Emotion and Walk This Way were released as singles in 1975. In the United States it became Aerosmith's commercially most successful studio album, with nine million copies sold according to the RIAA. In 2003 Rolling Stone placed it on its list of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/aerosmith-toys-in-the-attic.listen: Listen to Walk This Way and notice how the guitar riff and the rhythm of the drums alternate beneath the vocals.

werk/afrojack-take-over-control.text: In August 2010 DJ Afrojack from Spijkenisse released Take Over Control, with the singer Eva Simons. The song became a hit in the Netherlands and also reached the British Top 40. A few months later Afrojack, together with David Guetta, won a Grammy for a remix of Madonna. Around 2010, Dutch DJs like him became global stars in the popular EDM, electronic dance music.
werk/afrojack-take-over-control.listen: Hear the build-up to the drop, the moment when the beat and the sharp synthesizers suddenly come back in full force.

werk/agnetha-faltskog-elva-kvinnor-i-ett.text:
Elva kvinnor i ett hus was released on 1 December 1975 on Cupol as Agnetha Fältskog's fifth studio album. It had already been planned before 1973, but her pregnancy and the success of ABBA caused delays. She made it in between busy promotion and, for the first time, produced a whole album herself. She wrote almost all the music herself, with lyrics by Bosse Carlgren. Their plan for twelve women in one house, with an elaborate sleeve, fell through when money and time ran out. At the record company's request, a Swedish version of S.O.S. opened the album.

The melodies are more complex and more pop and rock than on her earlier schlager albums. Carlgren's lyrics are little stories, ironic, full of humour and sometimes daring. Critics praised her singing and the higher production quality. The album stayed on the chart for 53 weeks and reached number 11.
werk/agnetha-faltskog-elva-kvinnor-i-ett.listen: Listen to Doktorn! and notice how the lyrics tell a little story, with humour rather than seriousness.

werk/agnetha-faltskog-som-jag-ar.text:
The Swedish singer's third solo album was released at the end of 1970. Little Gerhard and Björn Ulvaeus, at the time her boyfriend, produced it together. It was recorded at Metronome Studios in Stockholm, in January and in September and October 1970. As on her second album, she wrote two songs herself, Om tårar vore guld and Jag ska göra allt. For a few covers she wrote the Swedish lyrics.

Om tårar vore guld is the best-known song. It was released as the first single and reached the top three of Svensktoppen, where it stayed for fifteen weeks. It was also a highlight of her performances during the summer folkparks tour. A Danish composer claimed that she had used 22 bars of his. The case dragged on until 1977 and ended in a settlement. She also recorded Jag ska göra allt in German.
werk/agnetha-faltskog-som-jag-ar.listen: Listen to Om tårar vore guld: notice the melody and the singing of the composer herself, the song that became so successful in Sweden.

werk/ahmad-jamal-happy-moods.text:
Happy Moods contains recordings from 1960 and was released on the Argo label. Ahmad Jamal plays piano here, with Israel Crosby on bass and Vernel Fournier on drums. It is therefore a trio, as the pianist often did.

The record has ten tracks. The repertoire consists of well-known songs by composers such as Cole Porter, Billy Strayhorn and Kurt Weill, supplemented by two of his own pieces, Excerpt from the Blues and Rhumba No. 2. The longest tracks are Pavanne and Little Old Lady; the shortest is Time on My Hands, which lasts less than two minutes. AllMusic gave the album three stars and wrote that it does nothing to undermine the position of those who feel that Jamal deserves a much higher standing than he usually receives.
werk/ahmad-jamal-happy-moods.listen: Listen to Time on My Hands, a song of less than two minutes, and notice how the pianist tells a complete musical story in so short a time.

werk/ahmad-jamal-jamal-at-the-penthouse.text:
Jamal at the Penthouse was recorded live at Nola's Penthouse Studio in New York and was released in 1959 on Argo Records. The album differs from other records by Ahmad Jamal. His trio, with bassist Israel Crosby and drummer Vernel Fournier, is here joined by a string orchestra of fifteen musicians under the direction of arranger and conductor Joe Kennedy. Jamal thereby leaves the usual trio format, although the trio itself remains present.

Scott Yanow of AllMusic gave it three out of five stars. He called it a change of pace: the interpretations are mostly beautiful, but offer enough variety to hold the attention. The repertoire includes standards such as Ivy by Hoagy Carmichael, alongside Ahmad's Blues by Jamal himself and Sophisticated Gentleman by Kennedy.
werk/ahmad-jamal-jamal-at-the-penthouse.listen: Listen to Ivy by Hoagy Carmichael and notice how the string orchestra complements the trio.

werk/ahmad-jamal-the-piano-scene-of-ahma.text:
The Piano Scene of Ahmad Jamal was released in 1959, but the recordings come from earlier years. They date from his first sessions for Okeh in Chicago in 1951 and 1952 and from a session for Epic in New York in October 1955. There are also tracks from the sessions for the 1956 album The Ahmad Jamal Trio. The record therefore shows how the pianist sounded at the beginning of his career.

The repertoire consists of standards and his own work, such as Old Devil Moon, Poinciana and Ahmad's Blues. The jazz historian Scott Yanow remarked that Jamal's use of space and dynamics was very different from that of any other jazz pianist of the time. According to him, the record shows a style that would have a great influence on the music of Miles Davis.
werk/ahmad-jamal-the-piano-scene-of-ahma.listen: Listen to Poinciana and notice how Jamal leaves space between the notes and how he lets the volume shift.

werk/air-10-000-hz-legend.text:
This second album by Air was released on 28 May 2001 in France on Virgin Records and a day later in the United States on Astralwerks. The French duo made the songs longer and more electronic than on earlier records. They also collaborated with other artists, including Beck and suGar Yoshinaga of Buffalo Daughter. The cover shows Monument Valley, on the border of Arizona and Utah.

The reactions were less favourable than for earlier records. Many reviewers missed the sound of Moon Safari from 1998, although the soundtrack of The Virgin Suicides from 2000 does resemble this album in atmosphere. The magazine Q nevertheless counted the record among the fifty best of 2001. The website Stereogum takes its name from a line in the lyrics of Radio Number 1.
werk/air-10-000-hz-legend.listen: Listen to Radio Number 1 and notice the lyrics: the website Stereogum is named after a line from this song. Can you hear which line it is?

werk/air-moon-safari.text:
Moon Safari is the debut of the French electronic duo Air, released in January 1998 by Source and Virgin Records. The album received wide praise on release. Alexis Petridis wrote in Mixmag that it creates a sound world of its own, glossier and chicer than reality. Other critics mentioned its sense of melody, its relaxed attitude and the bold use of the vocoder.

They praised above all the pop songs Sexy Boy and Kelly Watch the Stars, alongside more experimental work. The Face and Select chose it as album of the year. Moon Safari is regarded as the record that set the stage for the emerging downtempo, and anniversary editions appeared in 2008 and 2024.
werk/air-moon-safari.listen: Listen to Sexy Boy. Notice the vocoder voice and how relaxed the melody stays, even when the sound is tight and electronic.

werk/air-talkie-walkie.text:
Talkie Walkie, Air's third album, was released on 26 January 2004 on Virgin Records. According to an NME reviewer, the two Frenchmen played and programmed all the instruments themselves in Paris and sang all the vocals themselves too. Producer Nigel Godrich and arranger Michel Colombier gave the record a subtle touch in the final stage. Alpha Beta Gaga was originally recorded for Madonna's American Life.

The reactions were largely positive. Rob Sheffield of Rolling Stone called the album excellent and spoke of elegant, melancholic soundtrack music for imaginary films. Alone in Kyoto was on the soundtrack of the 2003 film Lost in Translation, and Run and Surfing on a Rocket were used in television, film and a computer game. Pitchfork placed the record twentieth among the best albums of 2004.
werk/air-talkie-walkie.listen: Listen to Alone in Kyoto, known from Lost in Translation, and notice the atmosphere. Why does this music fit a film so well?

werk/airto-moreira-i-m-fine-how-are-you.text:
I'm Fine, How Are You? is a 1977 album by the Brazilian drummer and percussionist Airto Moreira. Many guests play on the record: the singer Flora Purim, the saxophonist Tom Scott, the trombonist Raul de Souza and the bassist Jaco Pastorius, who can be heard on Nativity. The Uruguayans Ruben Rada and Hugo Fattoruso wrote a number of the songs.

The record is full of percussion and mixes Brazilian and Latin American rhythms with jazz. The first side includes La Tumbadora and The Happy People, the second side The Road Is Hard (But We're Going To Make It) and Celebration Suite. Fragments of Celebration Suite were later used as the basis for Samba de Janeiro, Bellini's 1997 hit.
werk/airto-moreira-i-m-fine-how-are-you.listen: Listen to Celebration Suite and notice the layers of percussion that together form a driving rhythm.

werk/al-di-meola-elegant-gypsy.text:
Elegant Gypsy is the second album by guitarist Al Di Meola. It was released in 1977 on Columbia Records, as the follow-up to his debut Land of the Midnight Sun. The music is a fast mix of jazz and rock, with lightning-fast electric riffs and lyrical acoustic passages. Latin themes also appear, including some from flamenco.

The piece Race with Devil on Spanish Highway grew out of You Really Got Me by The Kinks, the first song he tried to play on guitar as a child of eight or nine. Many guests play on it: Paco de Lucía, Jan Hammer, Barry Miles, Anthony Jackson, Steve Gadd, Lenny White and Mingo Lewis. The magazine Guitar Player awarded the album its prize for best guitar album of the year.
werk/al-di-meola-elegant-gypsy.listen: In Mediterranean Sundance, listen to the acoustic guitar of Paco de Lucía alongside that of Al Di Meola.

werk/al-green-back-up-train.text:
Back Up Train is the debut album of the American soul singer Al Green. It was released in 1967 on Hot Line Records, a label run by his school friends Palmer James and Curtis Rodgers, before he signed with Hi Records. On the cover his name is spelled Greene, although that is actually the correct spelling. The title song had already been released as a single in January 1967, under the band name Al Greene and The Soul Mates.

The album later got a second life. In 1972 it was reissued on Bell Records, and a single of Guilty became a Top 30 R&B hit. In 1999 a reissue followed on Arista. In 2005 Legacy released the album under its original title Back Up Train, with the 1967 cover.
werk/al-green-back-up-train.listen: Listen to Back Up Train, the title song that was already released as a single in January 1967, and notice how the young singer carries the song with his voice.

werk/al-green-green-is-blues.text:
Green Is Blues is the second studio album by the American singer and songwriter Al Green. Hi Records released it on 15 April 1969, two days after his twenty-third birthday. His debut Back Up Train had received a lukewarm reception in 1967. Among critics and fans, this album is regarded as his breakthrough.

For the first time he worked with Willie Mitchell, the main producer of the record. Joe Cuoghi, co-founder and president of Hi Records, supervised the sessions. The repertoire contains many covers, from My Girl and The Letter to Get Back by Lennon and McCartney. A connoisseur later wrote that the record ushered the Memphis Sound into a new era, thanks to the tight arrangements of the Hi Rhythm Section. It was the start of a studio partnership between the singer and Mitchell.
werk/al-green-green-is-blues.listen: Listen to Get Back, a song by Lennon and McCartney, and notice how the vocals and the band turn it into a soul song.

werk/al-green-i-m-still-in-love-with-you.text:
I'm Still in Love with You is Al Green's fifth studio album. It was released on 23 October 1972 on Hi Records, after recording sessions held that year. The producer was Willie Mitchell.

The album reached number 4 on the American album chart and number 1 on the R&B chart. Four singles came from it: Love and Happiness, I'm Still in Love with You and Look What You Done for Me. The last two became hits in the American top five. Love and Happiness is on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 greatest songs. The drum intro of I'm Glad You're Mine has been sampled more than two hundred times, including in Dead Wrong by The Notorious B.I.G. with Eminem. Rolling Stone also included the album on its list of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/al-green-i-m-still-in-love-with-you.listen: Listen to I'm Glad You're Mine and notice the drum intro at the start, because it has been sampled by many other artists.

werk/al-green-let-s-stay-together.text:
This fourth album by Al Green was released on 31 January 1972, as the follow-up to Al Green Gets Next to You. It was recorded at Royal Recording Studio in Memphis, under the direction of producer Willie Mitchell, for the third time. The accompaniment came from the Hi Rhythm Section, including the Hodges brothers, supplemented by horns and backing vocalists.

The title song became Green's trademark and his only pop number one. The album also contains his version of How Can You Mend a Broken Heart by the Bee Gees, which Q later described as the soul ballad taken to a new level of refinement. Critics above all praised the voice: Rolling Stone called it a marvel, one that can croon, shout and soar in a soft falsetto. The album topped the soul chart and ushered in his classic period, a series of acclaimed albums.
werk/al-green-let-s-stay-together.listen: Listen to Let's Stay Together and notice how Green moves his voice from soft and measured to a high falsetto.

werk/al-jarreau-this-time.text:
This Time was released in 1980 on Warner Bros. Records and was the fourth studio album by the jazz singer Al Jarreau. Jay Graydon produced the record. The sound shifted towards R&B, with synthesizers, Fender Rhodes and a horn section. Studio musicians such as bassist Abraham Laboriel and drummer Steve Gadd provided the rhythm section.

That change of course worked. It was his first album in the top 40 of the Billboard 200 and in the top 10 of the R&B chart, and it topped the jazz chart. Never Givin' Up earned a Grammy nomination in 1981 for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance. That award went to George Benson, who had just made a comparable change of style.
werk/al-jarreau-this-time.listen: In Never Givin' Up, listen to the voice: the singer does not merely sing the melody but also works as percussion. Notice how the horns and synthesizers around it create a polished sound.

werk/al-martino-i-love-you-because.text:
This is the sixth album by the American singer Al Martino and was released in 1963. That year it reached number 7 on the Billboard albums chart. The success came from the title song. I Love You Because topped the adult contemporary chart on 25 May 1963 and reached number 3 in the Hot 100 on 1 June.

The record has twelve songs, six on each side. They are short: no song lasts longer than about three minutes. Besides the title song, it includes Bouquet of Roses, Still, You Win Again, It's a Sin and Take These Chains from My Heart. The chart figures show that the singer reached a large audience in 1963, and with an album full of short, direct songs he managed it well.
werk/al-martino-i-love-you-because.listen: Listen to I Love You Because and notice how short and direct the song is: in less than three minutes the story is told.

werk/alan-price-between-today-and-yester.text:
Between Today and Yesterday was released in 1974 and is an autobiographical concept album. On the original LP the first side was called Yesterday and the second Today. The first side contains six songs about the working-class milieu in the north of England, where Alan Price grew up. They lean heavily on the style of the music hall. The second side contains six songs about the more modern Price, in a more contemporary sound.

He originally wrote the title song for the album Savaloy Dip, which had been recorded earlier but was not released until 2016. All the songs are his own. The album was both a commercial and a critical success.
werk/alan-price-between-today-and-yester.listen: Listen to Jarrow Song, on the Yesterday side, and notice the atmosphere of the old North of England. Then compare it with City Lights from the Today side.

werk/alanis-morissette-jagged-little-pil.text:
After two dance records, the Canadian singer was left without a record contract in 1993. She moved to Los Angeles and met producer Glen Ballard there. Within half an hour they were writing and experimenting together in his home studio. They tried to write and record one song a day, with few overdubs, and her vocals were recorded in one or two takes. The record was released through Maverick Records in June 1995.

It is an alternative rock record with influences from post-grunge, hip hop and pop, with guitars, harmonica and drum machines. The lyrics are about anger and failed relationships, and Ballard gave the raw emotions a pop feel. On You Oughta Know, Dave Navarro and Flea play. The album received good reviews and won five Grammys, including Album of the Year. She was then the youngest winner of that award. It is one of the best-selling albums ever.
werk/alanis-morissette-jagged-little-pil.listen: Listen to Perfect, the first song that was played for record executives: notice how simple it sounds, with just vocals and acoustic guitar.

werk/alanis-morissette-jagged-little-pil.text:
For the tenth anniversary of Jagged Little Pill, Alanis Morissette re-recorded her successful 1995 album. Producer Glen Ballard wrote string arrangements and gave the songs extra studio treatment. It became a largely acoustic version, available from 13 June 2005. At first the album was sold only at Starbucks in North America, which led to a quarrel with HMV Canada. The cover is a sepia-toned reference to that of the original.

Critics were generally negative. The album received 40 out of 100 points on Metacritic. Many reviewers felt that the anger and raw emotion of the original had disappeared and that the sharp edges had been softened. Others wondered why it was necessary, since Perfect and Mary Jane had already sounded acoustic in 1995. Hand in My Pocket became the single in the United States.
werk/alanis-morissette-jagged-little-pil.listen: Listen to Hand in My Pocket and set it beside the 1995 original. Can you hear what is left of the raw energy?

werk/alanis-morissette-supposed-former-i.text:
Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie is Alanis Morissette's fourth studio album, released on 3 November 1998 by Maverick Records. After an exhausting eighteen-month world tour for Jagged Little Pill, she retreated to India to recover. That journey gave the album its concept. The title comes from a line in So Pure, and the cover bears phrases from eight Buddhist precepts.

Her writing style became more complex and often departed from the fixed verse and chorus, sometimes like a stream of thought, with influences from trip hop and chamber rock. She wrote Baba and Thank U after the journey. Thank U reached the American top 20. The record went straight to number one in the United States, with the highest first-week sales figure a woman had achieved until then. In 2000 she won the Juno Award for Album of the Year with it.
werk/alanis-morissette-supposed-former-i.listen: Listen to Thank U and notice how calm and serene it sounds, while many listeners knew her from angry songs.

werk/alanis-morissette-under-rug-swept.text:
Under Rug Swept is Alanis Morissette's fifth studio album and was released in February 2002 on Maverick Records. It was the first album that she wrote and produced entirely herself. In Toronto she wrote seven songs in the first week, each in at most about twenty minutes, with the vocals recorded straight away in one or two takes. Production was delayed by disputes with Maverick's management. Label co-founder Madonna persuaded her to stay.

The album is about repairing relationships and bridging gaps between people. Opener 21 Things I Want in a Lover lists what she is looking for in a partner, partly as a joke. A Man is written from a male perspective, as an answer to Narcissus. Critics praised the lyrics, the rawness and the singing. The record reached number one on the Billboard 200 and in eleven other countries.
werk/alanis-morissette-under-rug-swept.listen: Listen to 21 Things I Want in a Lover and notice how humour and seriousness alternate.

werk/albert-ayler-love-cry.text:
Love Cry was released in 1968 on Impulse! Records. The album was recorded at Capitol Studios in New York, in August 1967 and February 1968, with Alan Silva on bass and Milford Graves on drums. It was the last record on which his brother Donald plays trumpet. Shortly after the session he left the band and returned to Cleveland. According to Phil Freeman, the record was partly an attempt by Impulse! to reintroduce the saxophonist to the public.

The saxophonist had earlier recorded Ghosts and Bells in much longer and wilder versions for ESP-Disk. Here they are short and focused on the melody, with influences from rhythm and blues and New Orleans polyphony. The harpsichord gives the music a strange sound. Universal Indians lasts almost ten minutes and is the big piece of the record. One reviewer called it one of his best records, another wrote that it is often overlooked.
werk/albert-ayler-love-cry.listen: Listen to Dancing Flowers and notice the trill of the harpsichord, which sounds like music for a silent horror film.

werk/albert-ayler-spirits-rejoice.text:
Saxophonist Albert Ayler recorded Spirits Rejoice in 1965 in New York, at Judson Hall, a hall hired solely for the recording, and so without an audience. The record was released on the ESP-Disk label. It was the last time bassist Gary Peacock played with him. Label founder Bernard Stollman asked for a short piece during the session. That is how Holy Family came about, less than three minutes long. Later Stollman felt that in doing so he had broken the agreement that the artist himself decides what his work contains.

The music sounds wild and loud, but follows a logic of its own. The title song borrows from La Marseillaise and is a long march of themes with harmonies for three horns, according to biographer Jeff Schwartz. One reviewer wrote that the music at first angered many experts. Steve Huey called the album one of the saxophonist's wildest and loudest records, but also saw in it a surprisingly predetermined structure.
werk/albert-ayler-spirits-rejoice.listen: Listen to D.C. and notice how the piece moves from a loud, fast and dense beginning into complete silence during the solos of the two bassists.

werk/ali-farka-toure-radio-mali.text:
Radio Mali consists of remastered selections from earlier albums by Ali Farka Touré, originally recorded between 1975 and 1980. The record has sixteen tracks, and he plays guitar on all sixteen. On most of them he also sings. On Bra Nabo and Fangha they play the n'jarka, a fiddle, and Nassourou Sare plays n'goni on a few tracks.

The album opens with Njarka, a fragment of less than a minute, and closes with a second, slightly longer fragment. The title track Radio Mali lasts less than three minutes. Short pieces and long tracks of more than six minutes thus alternate, such as Bandalabourou, Gambari and Amadinin. The record gives an overview of the work from his first years.
werk/ali-farka-toure-radio-mali.listen: Listen to Soko and notice how the n'goni of Nassourou Sare sounds alongside the guitar.

werk/ali-farka-toure-the-river.text:
The River is a double album that was released on 17 October 1980 on Columbia Records. Bruce Springsteen wanted to put the live sound of the E Street Band on record. Together with manager Jon Landau and band member Steven Van Zandt he produced the album during eighteen months of sessions in New York. He dropped a previously planned single LP, The Ties That Bind, because it did not fit his vision. In total more than fifty songs were recorded.

The record sounds like a rough garage band and combines party songs with reflective ballads. The lyrics are mostly about love, marriage and family. Hungry Heart became an American top ten hit, and Fade Away and The River were also released as singles. The River was his first album to top the American chart. Critics praised the songwriting and the band's playing, but others felt that he was repeating old material. Later it was regarded as one of his best works.
werk/ali-farka-toure-the-river.listen: Listen to Hungry Heart and notice how the band sounds: rough, cheerful and live.

werk/ali-farka-toure-the-source.text:
The Source by Ali Farka Touré was released on World Circuit in 1992. He sings on almost all the tracks and plays electric and acoustic guitar. On the opening track Goye Kur he also plays the n'jarka. Many guests play on it: Afel Bocoum sings, Hamma Sankare plays calabash, Oumar Touré congas, Nitin Sawhney tabla on Inchana Massina and Taj Mahal acoustic guitar on Roucky and Mahini Me.

The album topped the Billboard World Albums chart. The Los Angeles Times called Cinquante Six, an instrumental solo picking piece, one of the most impressive moments. There he lays a melody with a flamenco colour over a cleanly picked folk rhythm. Trouser Press wrote that the record challenges the singer to go beyond the blues, as in Hawa Dolo, and to play more complicated lines with just a few notes, as in Roucky.
werk/ali-farka-toure-the-source.listen: Listen to Cinquante Six, an instrumental piece for guitar alone, and notice how a picked folk rhythm is overlaid with a melody with a flamenco colour.
